analysis.one_liner: Limits the legal shield protecting internet platforms from lawsuits over user-generated content.
analysis.headline: The SAFE TECH Act never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill narrows Section 230, the 1996 law that shields websites and social media platforms from lawsuits over content their users post. Under the bill, platforms could be sued in civil rights, antitrust, stalking and harassment, international human rights, and wrongful death cases, and could not claim the shield for paid or platform-funded speech. A platform sued over user content would have to prove in court that the shield actually applies, and courts could order platforms to remove material likely to cause irreparable harm. The bill was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People harmed by content platforms carry or amplify: victims of online harassment and stalking, users facing discriminatory practices (for example, in housing or job ads), competitors claiming anticompetitive conduct, and families bringing wrongful death suits tied to online content. Consumer and civil rights plaintiffs generally regain a path to court that current law largely closes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of online harassment and discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Removes platform immunity in civil rights, antitrust, stalking, harassment, and wrongful death cases, letting victims and consumers sue over discriminatory or harmful conduct that current law blocks [S2][S3].
Strips the shield when a platform accepts payment to make speech available or creates or funds the speech itself, ending immunity for advertising-driven distribution of harmful content [S2][S3].
Requires a platform being sued to prove, as an affirmative defense, that its immunity applies — currently it can often win dismissal without that burden [S2][S3].
Lets courts order a platform to remove or restrict material likely to cause irreparable harm, while protecting the platform from liability for complying with such an order [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large online platforms — social networks, video sites, marketplaces, and ad-supported services — would face more lawsuits, higher legal defense costs, and more pressure to remove content preemptively. Litigation costs and compliance risk would fall hardest on platforms with the most user content, though any site hosting user speech would be exposed.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media and internet platforms

drawbacks.text: The bill makes the platform's immunity an affirmative defense it must prove in court [S3], which would push more cases past the early dismissal stage; even weak lawsuits would become costlier to defend, and platforms could respond by removing more legal speech to avoid suits.

The exception for speech the platform was paid to carry [S3] reaches far beyond targeted ads — it could strip protection from any monetized hosting, creating litigation exposure for a wide range of websites, not just the largest ones.

Plaintiffs could seek injunctions to force removal of material 'likely to cause irreparable harm' [S3], a standard that gives courts significant discretion over online speech and raises concerns about pressure on platforms to take down controversial but lawful content.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For victims of online harassment, discriminatory ad targeting, and other platform-enabled harms, current Section 230 law often means there is no lawsuit at all, so regaining access to court is a real and meaningful benefit. The cost is real too: more litigation against platforms, some of it meritless, and likely more aggressive content removal by companies trying to stay out of court. How the courts would apply the new carve-outs is genuinely uncertain. The bill is a targeted rework rather than a wholesale repeal, but it would substantially change the legal position of every site that hosts user content.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee ten days later, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the SAFE TECH Act on February 28, 2023, to narrow Section 230's liability shield for internet platforms [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S5].
On March 10, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce, where it stayed [S5].

The bill drew two cosponsors, both Democrats, and never advanced out of committee; the full action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large internet platforms — social networks, video services, and ad-supported sites — keep the broad legal immunity the bill would have narrowed, and no victims of online harassment or discrimination gained a new path to court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large social media and internet platforms

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to narrow Section 230 platform immunity [S1][S3].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats were ever attached to the bill and no Republican cosponsored it; since it never reached a vote, no actual support or opposition split was recorded [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would strip their Section 230 immunity in civil rights, harassment, antitrust, and wrongful death cases and for paid or funded speech [S2][S3], exposing them to suits they currently avoid. Their interest in keeping the shield runs against victims seeking recourse [S3].

The bill removes immunity for speech a platform was paid to make available [S3], which targets ad-funded distribution, including targeted ads that have been used to discriminate in housing and employment.
